content: Patients undergoing shorter multidrug-resistant tuberculosis (MDR-TB) treatment regimens, whether standardized or all-oral variants, require careful evaluation of treatment outcomes. It is also essential to explore the potential of next-generation rapid molecular testing not only for diagnostic purposes but also for monitoring treatment response. Additionally, engineering challenges related to the implementation of more cost-effective liquid culture systems should be thoroughly assessed. Decisions regarding the timing and type of surgical intervention for MDR-TB patients, particularly in the context of drug-resistance patterns, need to be more clearly defined. Furthermore, there is a need for improved data collection, reporting, and standardization concerning surgical outcomes, including long-term survival post-surgery. The risk of tuberculosis transmission in hospital-centered care versus outpatient clinics remains a critical question. Additional cost-effectiveness studies comparing decentralized and centralized care models are necessary. Systematic collection and publication of data on decentralized care are also required, as many programs provide such care but have not published their findings. The recommendations and remarks in the WHO policy guidelines on drug-resistant tuberculosis treatment are the result of collaborative efforts by professionals with extensive expertise in public health policy, program management, and patient care for drug-resistant tuberculosis (DR-TB). The WHO acknowledges their contributions and expresses gratitude for their time and support. The development of these guidelines involved separate Guideline Development Groups (GDGs) for each included guideline. The chairs of the GDG for the 2018 WHO treatment guidelines for isoniazid-resistant tuberculosis were Nancy Santesso (GRADE methodology specialist, Canada) and Kelly Dooley (clinical pharmacologist and infectious diseases specialist, United States). Other GDG members included experts in pediatrics, laboratory science, drug management, program management, and public health from various countries. The WHO also thanks the External Review Group (ERG) members for their valuable inputs during the review of the final guideline document. Observers and external partners, including representatives from international organizations and technical agencies, also contributed to the process. The systematic review team, led by experts from McGill University, Canada, conducted individual patient data analyses and developed GRADE evidence profiles. Their findings were presented to the GDG during discussions. The WHO Guideline Steering Committee, composed of staff from the WHO Global TB Programme and other departments, oversaw the development of the guidelines. The text was drafted and finalized following input from the GDG, ERG, and the WHO Guideline Steering Committee, before submission to the WHO Guideline Review Committee. Funding for the guideline development process was provided by the United States Agency for International Development (USAID) and other grants. The WHO acknowledges the financial support that enabled systematic reviews, GDG meetings, and guideline production. The 2018 update of the WHO treatment guidelines for multidrugand rifampicin-resistant tuberculosis (MDR/RR-TB) was based on discussions held by the GDG convened by the WHO Global TB Programme. The WHO expresses gratitude to the numerous MDR/RR-TB patients whose data informed the development of these guidelines. The WHO also acknowledges the contributions of the McGill University team and other experts who conducted systematic reviews and individual patient data analyses. The guideline development process was supported by funding from various sources, including the Russian Government and UNITAID. The 2011 update of the guidelines for the programmatic management of drug-resistant tuberculosis was coordinated by Dennis Falzon under the guidance of Ernesto Jaramillo and Léopold Blanc of the WHO Stop TB Department. Contributions from experts in clinical practice, program management, public health, and laboratory science were instrumental in the development of these guidelines.
